one_liner: C++11 callback wrapper over libuv with TCP/UDP/HTTP; ties Boost.Asio 1.67 on loopback echo, trails nginx on HTTP.
what_it_does: Wraps libuv's C API in C++11 classes (EventLoop, TcpServer, TcpClient, TcpConnection, Udp, Timer, TimerWheel, Async, DnsGet) that take std::function callbacks instead of C function pointers, plus a small HTTP/1.x server and client with a radix-tree router (wildcards and path parameters) and optional packet framing (Packet with head/end bytes and a 16-bit length). It is not a drop-in for Asio: you get libuv's single-threaded loop, a message callback receiving (connection, const char*, size), and write(buf, size, callback) on the connection. Cross-thread work goes through writeInLoop/runInThisLoop, which push a std::function onto a mutex-guarded queue and wake the loop with uv_async_send.
how_it_is_fast: There is no new I/O technique; it is libuv's epoll (Linux) or IOCP (Windows) reactor with a thin layer on top. Each connection reuses one std::string read buffer sized to libuv's 64 KB read suggestion, and write() hands the caller's pointer straight to uv_write without copying; libuv 1.30 attempts the write() syscall immediately when the write queue is empty, so an echo is one read callback plus one synchronous write. TCP_NODELAY is on by default for accepted and client sockets. Per message it still pays a shared_from_this refcount, two std::function hops and a heap-allocated WriteReq per write.
when_to_use: You already depend on libuv (or want its Linux epoll and Windows IOCP backends) but want C++11 lambdas and classes instead of raw uv_* handles and C callbacks.

Single-threaded TCP services with small-to-medium messages where a small, readable, MIT-licensed code base you can vendor matters more than peak throughput; heartbeat timeouts come built in via TimerWheel.

Internal tools that need a minimal HTTP/1.x endpoint with radix-tree routing (prefix wildcards, path values, query parameters) and no dependency beyond libuv, such as health checks or control endpoints.
Framed binary protocols that fit the bundled Packet/PacketBuffer format (head byte, end byte, payload up to 65,535 bytes).
when_not_to_use: You expect it to beat Asio: the published echo numbers are a tie (-1.9% to +8.1% versus Boost.Asio 1.67, single runs), and its HTTP server is about 9% slower than nginx 1.14.2 in the README's own ab screenshots.

Multi-core servers: an EventLoop is single-threaded and TcpServer has no multi-reactor or SO_REUSEPORT mode, so scaling means wiring your own loops per thread; libhv's 4-thread pingpong reports about 1.38x over plain libuv.

Production HTTP: the server closes the connection after every response (no keep-alive), has no TLS, sends nothing for unmatched routes or parse errors, caps requests at the 32 KB CycleBuffer by default, and has no static-file serving (issue #48 open).
Writers whose buffers do not outlive the call, or peers that read slowly: write() never copies and the connection keeps reading while writes queue, so there is no backpressure.
You need macOS/BSD support, coroutines or io_uring: the README lists Linux and Windows only and the API is callbacks only; for io_uring see uring_exec, Condy or Asio's io_uring backend.

integration.dependencies: libuv (libuv 1.30.0 headers plus prebuilt static libraries for gcc 8.3.0 and Windows SDK 10.0.10240 are checked into libuv1.30.0/, and CMakeLists.txt links that prebuilt libuv.a), pthread
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (CMakeLists.txt sets -std=c++11 -O2), CMake 2.8+; README build targets are VS2017, Code::Blocks and CMake on Linux; VS2015 build errors were reported (#23)
integration.platforms: Linux and Windows (README); Signal is Linux-only (#ifdef __linux__); macOS not documented
integration.thread_safety: One EventLoop per thread. TcpServer, CycleBuffer and ListBuffer are marked not thread-safe in the source, and write() must run on the loop thread (cross-thread write() crashed in #41); only writeInLoop and EventLoop::runInThisLoop are safe from other threads.

gotchas: write() never copies, while libuv requires the buffer to stay valid until the write callback. The library's own code ignores that: HttpServer writes each response from a local std::string, HttpClient writes the request from a local string (still so after the 2023 'fix http send' commit), the echo client writes from a stack array, and the README echo server writes straight from the connection's reused read buffer while reading continues. It works on Linux only because libuv writes immediately when the queue is empty; once a send buffer fills or a payload is large, the queued write reads freed or overwritten memory.

HTTP server: it needs HttpServer::SetBufferMode(CycleBuffer or ListBuffer) or it logs an error and serves nothing. The CycleBuffer is a fixed 32 KB ring whose append() failure is ignored, so a larger request is silently dropped and never answered. ListBuffer is a std::list<uint8_t>, one heap node per byte. Every response closes the connection.

writeInLoop() on a connection that has already gone calls the AfterWriteCallback without a null check, so passing nullptr there throws std::bad_function_call inside the loop. Heap corruption on client reconnect (#43, CentOS 7, uv-cpp 1.5.4) was never answered. Packet lengths are uint16_t (#30). With setTimeout() enabled, every received message inserts a shared_ptr into a std::set in the TimerWheel.

Harness flaws behind the README numbers (the numbers are not invalidated; with one message in flight per connection the zero-copy echo is safe): uv-cpp's sockets get TCP_NODELAY by default but the Boost.Asio harness never sets no_delay; the Asio side std::copies each read into a second 32 KB buffer and uses async_write_some, ignoring short writes; and each cell is one one-second printout. The one-client cells work out to about 14.6k-16.1k round trips per second for both libraries at every packet size (derived from page data), so they measure loopback wake-up latency, not library overhead.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick uv-cpp over libhv or evpp only if you specifically want libuv underneath a thin C++11 callback layer that is small enough to vendor and read in an afternoon. libhv reports about 1.37-1.38x over libevent and libuv in a 4-thread pingpong, and on Linux uring_exec (1.27-3.46x over Asio's io_uring backend) or PhotonLibOS are better-measured choices for throughput.
verified_claims_summary: The repo's echo_server/echo_client pair was run against an equivalent Boost.Asio 1.67 pair on one Intel Core i5-8265U laptop over loopback (Debian 8, gcc 8.3.0 -O2, libuv 1.30.0), with one one-second kbyte/s printout per cell. With one client, uv-cpp was within -1.9% to +1.6% of Asio across 1-8 KB messages; with 10-5000 clients at 4 KB it was 1.1% to 8.1% ahead. A separate ab run (1000 concurrency, 100,000 requests) has its HTTP server at 15,408 req/s against nginx 1.14.2's 16,946, about 9% slower (derived from page data).
status_note: MIT with 839 stars, but the last code change was 2023-12-23 (HttpClient only) and the last commit is a 2025-11-13 README edit, so 'active' holds only by the 12-month rule. The 2021 reconnect crash (#43) and the September 2026 benchmarking question (#58) have no maintainer reply. The README numbers date from about April 2020, are not pinned to a commit, and come from a harness with TCP_NODELAY only on uv-cpp's side and latency-bound one-client cells. Usable as a small vendorable wrapper, provided you keep every write buffer alive until its callback, which the library's own HTTP code does not.
